**What I added to make it a journal submission rather than a conference paper:**

**Four research questions**, stated explicitly and each answered with a measurement — TSE reviewers look for this structure and its absence reads as an unfocused paper.

**The full validity taxonomy**, which is the section a TSE reviewer reads hardest:

- **Construct** — the answer-key audit we independently verified, judge behaviour hand-adjudicated, and our loader deviation

**Plus a data availability statement** covering the byte-verified upstream pin, byte-identical prompts, two-method recomputation, and the reproduction protocol.

**Why TSE and not the others:** it is the only IEEE venue whose scope rewards rigor over novelty, it has no deadline, and the review cycle gives you time to run the powered replication that would fix the weak code-side section. **TSE** — [computer.org/csdl/journal/ts/about/14409](https://www.computer.org/csdl/journal/ts/about/14409):

> **entire-graph: A Deterministic, Zero-Inference Structural Index for Code and Conversational Memory**

The abstract opens on what entire-graph *is* — symbol and relation layers, content-derived identity, hybrid ranking, enforced context budget, byte-identical output, no model calls, no network — and only then evaluates it. entire-graph: A Deterministic Structural Index for
Code and Conversational Retrieval at Zero Inference Cost

entire-graph project

Entire

github.com/entireio/entire-graph

Abstract—We present entire-graph, a structural index that makes a corpus queryable by grammar-based parsing alone. It performs no language model calls and no network requests at index time, and produces a byte-identical index for a given corpus state. The system parses source files and prose documents into a graph of symbols, types, routes and document sections together with the relations between them, and answers queries by hybrid lexical and structural ranking under an enforced context budget. We describe the index model, the identity scheme that keeps symbol identifiers stable across unrelated edits, the ranking and candidate-selection algorithms, and the budget enforcement that bounds every response. We then report a defect in candidate selection that we found, characterised and corrected: admitting one candidate per file is correct for source code and wrong for prose, and it caused 200 returned results to carry only 19 distinct relevance scores, making cross-document evidence assembly structurally impossible. Finally we evaluate the system on a conversational-memory benchmark against six purpose-built memory systems, where it places first while consuming zero tokens to build its index against a measured 50.85 million for the strongest competitor. Because index construction is free, our claim is not that structural retrieval is more accurate than lexical retrieval, but that structure is worth having when structure costs nothing to build.

Index Terms—structural indexing, information retrieval, knowledge graphs, static analysis, deterministic systems, agent memory, performance evaluation.

I. Introduction

Retrieval systems for language agents face a corpus larger than the context window and must return the fragments that answer a question. Two design traditions address this.

The first, dominant in agent memory, pays a language model to read the corpus at ingest, extract facts or assemble a graph, and store the result [1], [2], [3]. A model normalises phrasing, resolves pronouns, and infers relations no parser recovers. The cost is a call per stored item, paid again whenever a document changes.

The second, standard in program analysis for over a decade, parses the corpus with a grammar and builds a structure directly [4], [5], [6]. It calls no model, and given a corpus state it produces the same index every time.

entire-graph belongs to the second tradition. This paper describes it: what it builds, how it ranks, how it bounds a response, and what happens when an index designed for source code is pointed at a corpus of conversation. The evaluation in Section VII is one section of the paper rather than its purpose.

A. Three properties that shape everything else

No inference at index time. No model is called while building the index. There is no extraction pass, no model-computed embedding, no summarisation. Construction is parsing and graph assembly. The consequence is not only cost: the index has no sampling step, so it cannot vary between builds.

Determinism. A given corpus state yields a byte-identical index. This is what allows the system to be used as a measurement instrument, and it is a property no extraction pipeline can offer, because a model's output for an unchanged input is not guaranteed stable across time or provider.

No egress. Both construction and query are local. There is no network path in either direction, which makes the system usable on corpora that cannot leave a machine.

B. Contributions

We describe the index model and its identity scheme (Section III); the query pipeline, including the ranking function, candidate selection and budget enforcement (Section IV); the corpus gate that decides whether a body of text is treated as code or prose, and the consequences of that decision (Section V); the query surface and implementation (Section VI); an evaluation against six memory systems including a directly metered index-construction cost comparison (Section VII); and a candidate improvement that we implemented, measured and rejected (Section VII-F).

II. System Overview

A corpus is a directory tree. Index construction walks it, dispatches each file to a grammar by extension, and runs a language-specific extraction pass that emits two record types: symbols, which are addressable regions of a file, and relations, which are directed edges between symbols or between a symbol and an endpoint outside the corpus.

A query is a natural-language string. Query processing scores candidate regions against it, selects a subset under a diversity rule, and assembles snippets under a byte ceiling. The response is a ranked list of regions, each carrying its file, line range, score, and the text itself.

The system is used both as a library and as a command-line tool. All results in this paper come from the command-line search verb, which is the interface an agent invokes.

III. The Index

A. Parsing

Files are parsed with tree-sitter grammars, which produce concrete syntax trees and recover from malformed input rather than failing. Recovery matters at corpus scale: a repository usually contains files that do not parse cleanly under any single grammar version, and an indexer that aborts on them indexes nothing.

Parsing is bounded by a profile. The system exposes three: a syntax-only profile that emits symbols without resolving relations, a fast profile that resolves relations shallowly, and a full profile that favours resolution correctness over latency. Profiles exist because relation resolution dominates construction cost, and a caller locating a definition does not need the same fidelity as a caller computing a blast radius.

B. Symbols and identity

Each grammar contributes an extraction pass emitting symbol records: functions, methods, classes, types, constants, routes, and for prose formats, document sections. A symbol carries a kind, a qualified name, a source range, a signature where one exists, its language, and its container.

Identity is content-derived rather than positional. A symbol's identifier is computed from its qualified name and containment path rather than from its byte offset or its index within a file. The practical consequence is that inserting a function at the top of a file does not renumber every symbol below it. Identifiers therefore survive ordinary editing, which is what makes two indexes of adjacent commits comparable at entity granularity, and what allows an index to be updated incrementally rather than rebuilt.

For prose formats the extraction pass emits one section record per heading. A markdown document with twelve headings yields twelve addressable regions. Nothing about this path is special-cased: the same machinery that emits a function record per declaration in a source file emits a section record per heading in a document.

C. Relations

Relations are emitted between symbols and between symbols and external endpoints. The families that carry retrieval signal are calls, inheritance and interface satisfaction, field and attribute access, type usage in parameters and return positions, imports, route handling, and containment.

Each relation records a resolution status and a confidence. An unresolved endpoint, for instance a call into a dependency outside the indexed tree, is retained as an external reference rather than dropped, because its presence is informative even when its target is not indexed: a function calling six external endpoints is differently characterised from one calling none.

Relation extraction is static and therefore incomplete by construction. Dynamic dispatch, reflection, runtime registration, decorators and code generation all produce edges no parser recovers. We treat this as a stated property of the approach rather than a defect to be worked around, and Section IX returns to it.

D. Determinism and incremental construction

Two indexes built from the same corpus state are byte-identical. This follows from having no sampling step anywhere in construction: parsing is deterministic, extraction is a pure function of the syntax tree, and identity is content-derived.

The system maintains a durable index over a committed corpus state, keyed so that an unchanged state reuses the cached index and a changed state rebuilds. Query against the working state is possible and is the default, so uncommitted edits are visible to search, at the cost of not reusing the cache.

IV. Query Processing

A. Ranking

A query is scored against candidate regions by a hybrid function combining lexical match over region bodies and identifiers, with tokenisation aware of camel case and snake case so that a query for user id matches userID and user_id; match against signatures and qualified names, which are weighted above body text because a name is a stronger signal of intent than an incidental mention; path and container signals; and graph proximity to regions already matched, which is where the relation layer enters ranking rather than merely serving traversal queries.

B. Candidate selection

Scoring produces more candidate regions than a response can carry, so a selection step decides which are eligible. The original rule admitted one region per file.

For source code this is deliberate and correct. A developer searching a repository wants distinct files, not nine fragments of the same function, and returning nine fragments of one function is the classic failure of a naive lexical index.

For prose it is wrong, and the failure is more serious than returning too little. Consider a corpus of documents each containing many relevant sections. Under one-region-per-file, the response carries the best region of each document, and every other region inherits its parent's position. Because the surviving regions are ordered by their parent document's score, a consumer sorting the response by relevance receives contiguous blocks, one per document.

Truncating that response to the top k, which any consumer with a context budget does, therefore yields the first document or two in their entirety rather than the best regions across the corpus. Evidence that must be assembled from several documents cannot surface. This is a structural impossibility rather than a probabilistic disadvantage: no amount of ranking improvement fixes it, because the ordering itself is degenerate.

The corrected rule makes the section the retrieval unit for prose. A section competes on its own score, exactly as an independent file would, keyed by its own identity and falling back to file path where a document has no section structure.

Ranking sections purely by score, however, reintroduces a different failure. A document whose sections all score well can crowd out a document holding the single region a query needs. We observed this during development, where a four-document corpus at a budget of six returned regions from only three documents. The selection rule therefore admits regions in two passes.

Algorithm 1: candidate selection
input: scored regions R, budget k
  S ← ∅; seen ← ∅
  breadth pass: for each document d in R,
    admit the highest-scoring region of d
    while |S| < k; mark d in seen
  merit pass: admit remaining regions in
    descending score order while |S| < k
output: S

The breadth pass binds every selection round rather than only the first, which is what prevents a high-scoring document from monopolising the budget in later rounds. Document coverage under the corrected rule is identical to the original, at 18.9 documents per query in our measurements, while distinct relevance scores rise from 17.1 to 84.9.

C. Budget enforcement

Every response is bounded by a maximum size in bytes. The bound is enforced during snippet assembly rather than afterwards, so a response is never constructed and then truncated.

Where a pass expands or rewrites spans, the ceiling is computed before the pass runs, and each expansion is committed individually and reverted if it would breach the ceiling. Post-pass text can therefore never exceed pre-pass text. This is a stronger guarantee than a post-hoc check and it is what allows a measured improvement to be attributed to selection rather than to a larger response.

The property is easy to get wrong in a way that looks correct. An early version of an expansion pass bounded itself on the serialised response rather than on snippet text. Because the structural envelope of a result is far larger than a prose snippet, discarding duplicate results freed envelope bytes that do not exist as text, and the pass spent them on real text: the serialised payload shrank while the text delivered to the consumer grew by 90 percent. Bounding on the wrong meter produces a result that appears rigorous and is not.

V. Code and Prose in One Index

A. The corpus gate

Whether a corpus is treated as code or prose is detected rather than declared. A corpus enters the prose path when it contains at least four units and at least 80 percent of its paths carry document extensions. Below that threshold the prose path does not activate and selection behaves exactly as it does for source code.

The gate is why the selection change described above is inert on a source repository. We verified this rather than assuming it: fifteen locate queries against a 300,000-line repository, at budgets of 10 and 50, comparing entire structured responses including statistics and diagnostics, produced 30 of 30 identical payloads. Three deliberately documentation-flavoured queries against the same repository returned zero regions carrying the prose retrieval mode.

B. Conversation as a corpus

Applying the index to conversation requires exactly one design decision: what is a document and what is a section. We map a conversational session to a document and a turn to a section, writing the transcript to markdown with a heading per turn and session metadata as front matter, so that every section inherits its session's date.

No conversational preprocessing occurs. There is no entity resolution, no coreference pass, no temporal normalisation, no fact extraction, no summarisation. The corpus is the transcript. This is worth stating plainly because it is what the evaluation tests: whether a structural index over raw transcripts is competitive with systems that spend hours of inference building structured representations of the same material.

VI. Query Surface and Implementation

The command-line surface exposes a small set of verbs, each answering a question a caller actually has: search locates regions for a natural-language query; impact returns the blast radius of changing one symbol, combining direct and transitive callers, callees, type consumers, data flows, and files that historically change alongside it; neighbors returns one relation family in one direction; diff reports entity-level change between two corpus states with a dependent count per changed entity; and snapshot streams the entire graph for ingestion elsewhere.

Output is available as human-readable text or as structured records. Bulk verbs stream rather than materialise, so memory is bounded by record size rather than by corpus size.

The implementation is a single static binary. Grammars are compiled in, so there is no runtime grammar download and therefore no network dependency and no version skew between the parser and the grammar. Unparseable files surface as machine-readable partial failures rather than silent omissions, which matters because a silently incomplete index is worse than an index that reports its gaps.

VII. Evaluation

We evaluate the system on LoCoMo [21], a long-conversation question-answering benchmark of ten multi-session conversations and 1,540 questions, against six memory systems built for that task. A memory system ingests the conversations and, per question, returns the evidence it judges relevant; a reader model answers from that evidence and a judge model scores the answer.

A. Protocol

Every system shares the same reader model, the same judge model, the same retrieval budget of 200 items, the same questions, and the same corpora. A guard exits on any asymmetric setting. The reader and judge prompts are byte-identical to the upstream harness; we did not author or tune the grading. Scores are read from each run's own aggregate rather than re-derived.

Ingest is native per system and deliberately not equalised: entire-graph calls no model, the extraction systems call one or two per chunk. That asymmetry is the property under measurement.

The comparison against the strongest competitor was run concurrently, in the same window, against the same endpoint. This matters: we measured 2.21 points of drift on an identical configuration re-run 26 hours apart, with byte-identical retrieval on 299 of 300 questions. Run-to-run noise is 0.65 points, established by running one system twice under identical settings.

B. Accuracy

Table I. LoCoMo, all 1,540 questions

Reported in its favour. b Its extraction model could not be established from surviving records; we read 77.60 as a lower bound and disclose the gap.

entire-graph places first. Its margin over the strongest competitor is 0.91 points with a discordant split of 43 to 29 and McNemar p = 0.125; we report the ranking and do not claim statistical significance for that margin. Its margin over the remaining five, from 1.9 to 17.1 points, is well clear of the 0.65-point noise floor. By category it leads three of four, with single-hop (p = 0.035) the one cell clearing significance alone.

C. Retrieval quality

Accuracy conflates retrieval with generation. Separating them produces the most useful result in this section: across every system tested, the probability of a correct answer given that gold evidence was retrieved is 0.96 to 0.97. The reader is saturated, so the benchmark discriminates on retrieval and very little else.

The 25-point gap at rank 10 is the largest separation we measure, and rank 10 is the regime that governs behaviour under a tight budget. We are not first on every retrieval metric: measured as gold items recovered per thousand characters returned, we are third, and the strongest competitor is markedly more efficient below roughly 25,000 characters because its units are distilled sentences where ours are prose spans.

D. Index construction cost

Table II. Measured index construction cost, full corpus

Linearity was tested rather than assumed, using two conversations of different length per system: the two extraction systems are exactly 1.00 and 2.00 calls per chunk, agreeing to 1.3 and 4.2 percent. One system is not projectable, its two conversations differing by 114.8 percent because its step count is chosen by its own agent loop rather than by chunk count; a replicate confirmed this is a property rather than an artifact, so we report per-conversation figures and no corpus total.

Call count is not a proxy for cost: cognee makes twice mem0's calls and spends four times fewer tokens. In wall-clock, the systems calling no model build in 4 to 7 seconds and the extraction systems in 3,373 to 20,478 seconds. The three-order-of-magnitude gap between the classes is the robust result; the ordering within the deterministic class spans 2.7 seconds on a shared machine and we do not treat it as established.

E. Effect of candidate selection

The isolated effect of promoting discarded regions, paired across all 1,540 questions with the binary as the only variable, is 2.27 points with a discordant split of 46 to 11 and McNemar p = 3.3 × 10−6. Treating sections as independent candidates adds a further 0.91. Together they take the system from 91.56 to 94.74 while returning 11.4 percent fewer bytes, because the earlier build computed regions and discarded them unread.

F. An improvement we measured and rejected

Residual failures cluster in a specific way. The system never failed to retrieve the correct session: the gold session appeared in 32 of 32 losses and 46 of 46 wins. What it missed was the correct turn, and 70 percent of missing gold turns sat within two turns of a region already returned. That is the signature of a retrieval unit smaller than the unit of meaning, since a conversational turn often opens with a pronoun whose referent lives in the preceding turn.

The obvious remedy is to expand each region into its neighbours, paying for the expansion by deduplicating text already returned. We implemented it and do not ship it. Measured across all 32 losing questions against an unchanged control, gold turns recovered rose from 21 of 51 to 23 of 51: one converted question in 32, at non-increasing bytes throughout. The premise is right and the economics are not, because there is not enough duplicated text to fund the expansion.

VIII. Related Work

Deterministic structural indexes over source are mature: code property graphs [4] unify syntax, control flow and data dependence; CodeQL [5] exposes a relational query language over an extracted database; stack graphs [6] resolve names incrementally at scale. A recent wave wraps such indexes for agents [13], [14], [15], [16], [17]. entire-graph belongs to this family; what is unusual here is applying it to conversation unchanged.

In agent memory, systems overwhelmingly build by inference [1], [2], [3], [7], [8], [9]. Recent work questions whether that inference is load-bearing: deterministic memory at comparable accuracy [10], zero-token memory operations [11], and a lexical interface over the unmodified archive that tops a memory benchmark [12].

Retrieval granularity is settled ground. Finer units outperform passages, and the advantage widens under a fixed budget [19]; hierarchical retrieval over a summary tree is established [20]. The selection rule in Section IV-B is an instance of that principle, not a new technique. What we contribute is the characterisation of its failure mode under per-document deduplication, which we have not seen named.

Two recent results argue lexical retrieval matches structured retrieval, on code [18] and on conversation [12], and both attack structured methods principally on the overhead of building and maintaining an index. We do not dispute the accuracy half of that argument; our margin cannot carry a dispute. We observe that the attack targets a cost this system does not incur.

IX. Limitations

Static extraction is incomplete. Dynamic dispatch, reflection, runtime registration and code generation produce edges no parser recovers. On prose this matters little; on code it bounds what the index can know, and it is the principal reason a structural index is a complement to execution-derived information rather than a replacement for it.

Context efficiency. Our units are prose spans where an extraction system's are distilled sentences, so we deliver roughly 30 percent more text at the same nominal budget and are decisively less efficient below about 25,000 characters. Closing that gap means shorter units, which means distillation, which means inference at index time. That trade should be made deliberately if it is made at all.

Evaluation scope. One benchmark, one reader model, one judge model. Generality across benchmarks and model families is not established here. The margin over the strongest competitor (p = 0.125) does not clear significance, and paired margins on this harness decay systematically with sample size, so subset results in this area should be treated as provisional, including our own interim readings.

Provenance. One competitor row could not be attributed to a specific extraction model from surviving records. The gap exists because we did not capture the benchmark runs with session recording, which would have committed model, endpoint and environment automatically. We disclose it rather than presenting the row as better attributed than it is.

X. Conclusion

entire-graph builds a queryable structural index by parsing alone. It calls no model, makes no network request, and produces a byte-identical index for a given corpus state. Its retrieval unit for prose is the document section, admitted under a two-pass rule that interleaves regions by merit while preserving document coverage, and every response is bounded by a ceiling computed before assembly rather than checked after it.

Applied to conversation with a single mapping decision and no preprocessing, it places first among seven systems on a conversational-memory benchmark, recovering all gold evidence by rank 10 on 82.0 percent of questions against 56.8 percent for the next measurable system, while consuming zero tokens to build its index against a measured 50.85 million for the strongest competitor.

We close on the narrow claim rather than the broad one. We do not argue that structural retrieval is more accurate than lexical retrieval; the evidence for that is contested and our own margin cannot settle it. We argue that an index which is free to build and free to rebuild does not need to win an accuracy argument to be worth having. That is the case this system makes, and Section VII-D is the measurement behind it.

**Three new diagrams, all showing mechanism rather than decorating:**

**Fig 1, the pipeline** — corpus, parse, extract, graph, query, with the dashed box marking the span that involves no model call and no network request.

**Fig 2, the graph on a two-file example** — actual nodes and edges, `HANDLES_ROUTE`, `CALLS`, `RETURNS_TYPE`, so the model stops being abstract.

**Fig 3, candidate selection** — the paper's technical core, side by side. Ranked regions per document, then what one-per-file keeps versus what section-as-candidate keeps, with the explanation of why a stable sort over four distinct scores makes cross-document evidence unreachable.

**And there's an algorithm block** for the two-pass selection rule, which is the thing a reader would otherwise have to reconstruct from prose.

**New content that wasn't in the old paper at all:** the profile system and why relation resolution dominates construction cost, content-derived identity and why it survives editing, resolution status and confidence on edges, incremental construction and cache keying, the tokenisation detail that makes `user id` match `userID`, and the full budget-enforcement argument including the serialised-payload mistake as a worked example of bounding on the wrong meter.

**The claim it closes on** is the narrow one: we don't argue structural retrieval beats lexical retrieval, because that's contested and our margin can't settle it. We argue an index that's free to build and free to rebuild doesn't need to win that argument.

IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering

```

input.prompt:
CAVEMAN-ULTRA COMPRESSED OUTPUT. Use rtk. Dense facts only.

VM `graphbench-g` zone `us-east1-b`. SSH: `gcloud compute ssh graphbench-g --zone=us-east1-b --tunnel-through-iap --command '...'` (auth refreshed; old ControlMaster socket is dead). Harness `$HOME/mem0harness`. **Box is idle — nothing is running.**

## Why this matters
We are preparing a journal submission arguing that a deterministic structural index is worth having
because it is free to build. **Two recent papers argue the structure itself is unnecessary**, and a
reviewer will demand a lexical baseline before believing us:

- *Better Call Grep* (ISSTA 2026, arXiv:2601.23254): naive grep-based retrieval "achieves performance
  comparable to sophisticated graph-based baselines" for repository-level code completion.
- arXiv:2608.12888 (filed 13 Aug 2026): a lexical, turn-granularity index over the **unmodified**
  conversation archive, building **no semantic structure at all**, tops MemoryAgentBench (58.2 vs
  HippoRAG 2's 53.2) and reaches 93.2 on LongMemEval-S.

**This baseline may beat us. That is the point.** Run it honestly. A result that undercuts our thesis
is far more valuable found by us now than by a reviewer later. Do not tune it against LoCoMo, do not
select a favourable variant, and do not stop early if it is doing well.

## Task: add a BM25-only arm and run it on LoCoMo

**1. Implement `bm25_client.py`** in `benchmarks/common/`, following the interface of the existing
adapters (`graphify_client.py` and `cmm_client.py` are the closest models — read them first). It must
implement the same `add()` / `search()` contract every other arm uses.

Design it to be a *fair strong baseline*, not a strawman:
- Index the **same corpus bytes** every other arm ingests. Verify byte-identity with md5 against the
  entire-graph arm's corpus, as the other ports did.
- **Turn granularity** — one indexed unit per conversational turn, matching what arXiv:2608.12888
  found effective. Report the unit count so it is comparable to the granularity table (entire-graph
  default is 19 units for conversation 0; mem0 stores 312; cmm 438).
- Standard BM25 (k1≈1.2, b≈0.75, stated in the report), stopword handling and tokenisation as
  conventional as possible. Use a well-known implementation (`rank_bm25` or equivalent) rather than
  writing your own scorer, and record which.
- **Zero LLM calls at ingest**, like ours. It belongs in the deterministic class.
- `search()` must **raise** on a missing buffer rather than return an empty list. That empty-buffer
  defect silently destroyed a competitor's score by 13.77 points earlier in this campaign.

**2. Wire it** into `make_memory_client` and the `--backend` choices of `benchmarks/locomo/run.py`.

**3. Run full LoCoMo n=1540** with the standard spine:
```
--provider azure_ai --answerer-model gpt-5.6-sol --judge-model gpt-5.6-sol
--top-k 200 --top-k-cutoffs 200,50,20,10
--max-workers 3 --question-workers 10 --rpm 60    LLM_TIMEOUT=600  FAIR_MODE=1
--project-name full_bm25
```
State root under `$HOME`, never `/tmp`. One process per project name, verified with
`ps -eo args | grep` (`pgrep -f` self-matches the SSH argv).

## Gates, applied honestly
- Void if drops exceed 1%, or if zero-context retrievals cluster by conversation.
- Verify at n≈30 and n≈100 that retrieval is non-empty and accuracy is plausible. **If it is
  anomalously low, that is a broken port, not a weak baseline** — diagnose before continuing. Three
  competitors in this campaign were suppressed by defects in their own code and we fixed all three
  in their favour. Hold this arm to the same standard.

## Report
- Implementation choices: library, parameters, tokenisation, unit granularity, units per conversation.
- Corpus byte-identity evidence.
- Full n=1540 score, per category (single-hop 841, multi-hop 282, temporal 321, open-domain 96),
  drops, zero-context count.
- Items and chars returned per question, so it slots into the retrieved-context table.
- Your honest read: does a purely lexical index match the structural one on this benchmark?

For reference, the arms it will sit beside: entire-graph 94.74, mem0 93.83, cognee 92.86, cmm 91.30,
graphify 87.34, letta 80.58, supermemory 77.60.

Do not disturb `results/` or `timings/` for existing arms. Report the number whatever it is.

input.description: Re-score banked retrievals with a second reader and judge
input.prompt:
CAVEMAN-ULTRA COMPRESSED OUTPUT. Use rtk. Dense facts only.

VM `graphbench-g` zone `us-east1-b`. SSH: `gcloud compute ssh graphbench-g --zone=us-east1-b --tunnel-through-iap --command '...'`. Harness `$HOME/mem0harness`. Box is idle apart from one other agent adding a BM25 arm; coordinate by keeping concurrency low.

## Why this matters
We are preparing a journal submission whose results use **one reader model and one judge model**
(`gpt-5.6-sol` for both). That is the single most likely reviewer objection: the ranking may be
specific to that model, and using one model as both reader and judge is a self-grading confound.

**The fix is cheap because we do not need to re-ingest or re-retrieve.** Every banked run stores the
full retrieved context per question. We can hold retrieval fixed and swap only the reader and the
judge, which isolates the reader's contribution exactly.

## The data
`$HOME/mem0harness/results/locomo/predicted_<project>/convN_qM.json`, schema:
```
question_id, category, question, ground_truth_answer, evidence,
retrieval: { search_query, search_results: [ {memory, score, id} ], total_results },
cutoff_results.top_200: { judgment, score, generated_answer, memories_evaluated, reason }
```
The arms to re-score, both complete at n=1540, same window:
- `predicted_sw_eg_mr3` — entire-graph, 94.74
- `predicted_sw_mem0b` — mem0 OSS, 93.83

## Task

**1. Establish what models are available** on the configured endpoint (`$HOME/.azenv`). We need at
least one reader distinct from `gpt-5.6-sol`, and ideally one that is not from the same family. List
what you find. If only one model is deployed, say so immediately and stop — that is a blocking
finding, not something to work around.

**2. Re-answer and re-judge both arms on their existing retrieved context.** Build the answering
prompt exactly as the harness does (`benchmarks/locomo/prompts.py::get_answer_generation_prompt`,
called from `run.py`) so the only variable is the model. Do not re-run retrieval. Do not re-ingest.

Run the factorial you can afford, in this priority order:
  a. **reader B + judge A** — isolates the reader
  b. **reader A + judge B** — isolates the judge, and directly tests the self-grading confound
  c. **reader B + judge B** — the fully independent replication

**3. Report per configuration:** overall score for each arm, the paired delta between arms, the
discordant split, and McNemar p. Per category if the budget allows.

## The question this answers
**Does entire-graph still lead mem0 under a different reader?** If the ranking flips, that is a
critical finding and must go in the paper. If it holds across readers, it is the strongest robustness
evidence in the submission and removes the reviewer's objection outright.

Report either result plainly. A flipped ranking found by us is a finding; found by a reviewer it is a
retraction.

## Constraints
- Read-only on `results/` and `timings/`. Write new output under `$HOME` outside the results tree.
- Throughput: `--question-workers 10 --rpm 60`, `LLM_TIMEOUT=600`. The harness defaults saturate the
  endpoint and collapse throughput.
- Watch for empty generated answers clustered at the start of a run: that is a cold-start connect
  timeout, worth 0.65 points, and it must not be mistaken for model weakness.
- Judge failures record as an empty `reason` field with a WRONG judgment. Count them and treat them
  as failed measurements rather than wrong answers.

Report the model inventory first, before running anything, since it determines what is possible.

content.text:
Both running. **Third addition, LongMemEval, is queued rather than launched** — our own measurements say three concurrent arms is the ceiling before endpoint contention starts corrupting results, and I'd rather not reintroduce the defect we spent hours finding.

**Two things block the arXiv submission, and both are yours to decide:**

**1. Authorship.** The paper currently says "entire-graph project," which arXiv will reject. It needs real author names and an affiliation. Who goes on it, and in what order?

**2. Licence.** arXiv asks at submission and it's effectively permanent:

- **arXiv perpetual non-exclusive** — the conservative default, keeps all rights, allows the TKDE submission cleanly
- **CC BY 4.0** — maximally reusable, best for citation and for a paper whose point is reproducibility
- **CC BY-NC-SA** — non-commercial only, which sits awkwardly with a paper about a product

I'd take the arXiv default or CC BY. IEEE permits preprints either way, so neither compromises TKDE.

- **path and container signals**
- **graph proximity** to already-matched regions, which is the structural half

# Retrieval and Search: A Study Pack

**Built from a real evaluation campaign, August 2026.** Everything here is either standard IR
knowledge you need, or something we measured directly and can defend. Where a number came from our
own runs it is marked **[measured]**. Where a claim is contested or uncertain it says so.

Written for someone preparing for a research engineering role in search and retrieval.

---

# PART 1 — entire-graph, the system

## 1.1 What class of system it is

entire-graph is a **sparse-lexical plus structural hybrid retriever with no learned component**. It
builds a queryable index by parsing a corpus with grammars, calling no language model and making no
network request, and producing a byte-identical index for a given corpus state.

Where it sits in the standard taxonomy:

| retrieval family | canonical examples | entire-graph |
|---|---|---|
| sparse lexical | BM25, TF-IDF, query likelihood | **yes** |
| learned sparse | SPLADE, uniCOIL, DeepImpact | no |
| dense bi-encoder | DPR, ANCE, Contriever, E5 | no |
| late interaction | ColBERT, ColBERTv2 | no |
| cross-encoder rerank | monoBERT, monoT5, RankT5 | no |
| structural / graph | PageRank, HITS, spreading activation | **yes** |

**It is first-stage retrieval only.** There is no second-stage reranker. That absence is the first
thing an IR interviewer notices, and the honest answer is that first stage plus reranker is the
standard architecture and this system implements the first half.

## 1.2 The index

**Documents** are files. **Retrievable units** are regions: a function, method, class, type, route,
or for prose a heading-delimited section.

This is **passage-level retrieval with syntactic boundaries**. Most RAG systems chunk by token count
with overlap, which cuts through semantic units arbitrarily. Here the boundaries come from a grammar,
so a passage is always a whole function or a whole section. A function is never split in half.

**Identity is content-derived**, computed from qualified name and containment path rather than byte
offset. Inserting a function at the top of a file does not renumber everything below it. In IR terms
this is a **stable docid under corpus mutation**, which is what makes incremental indexing possible.

**Relations** are typed directed edges: calls, inheritance, field access, type usage in parameters
and returns, imports, route handling, containment. Each carries a resolution status and a confidence.
Unresolved endpoints (a call into an unindexed dependency) are retained as external references rather
than dropped, because their presence is informative.

**Static extraction is incomplete by construction.** Dynamic dispatch, reflection, runtime
registration, decorators and code generation produce edges no parser recovers. This is a property of
the approach, not a defect, and it is why structural indexing complements execution-derived
information rather than replacing it.

## 1.3 Ranking signals

Hybrid scoring over four families:

1. **Lexical match** on bodies and identifiers, with subword tokenisation. camelCase and snake_case
   are split, so a query for `user id` matches `userID` and `user_id`.
2. **Field weighting.** Signatures and qualified names weigh above body text. This is fielded
   retrieval, the same idea as **BM25F**: a term in a title is worth more than a term in the body.
3. **Path and container signals.**
4. **Graph proximity** to already-matched regions. This is the structural half and it has no clean
   canonical name. It is *not* PageRank, which is a query-independent prior. It is closer to
   **spreading activation** over a typed graph, or to query expansion along edges.

## 1.4 Candidate selection, and the mechanism to know cold

Scoring produces more candidates than a response can carry, so a **selection** step decides
eligibility. Selection is a **diversification** problem, and diversification has a canon: **MMR**
(Carbonell and Goldstein, SIGIR 1998) trades relevance against novelty. Web search calls the same
thing **site collapsing**: do not return ten results from one domain.

entire-graph's original rule was diversification at its extreme setting: **one region per file,
always**. For code this is correct. A developer wants distinct files, not nine fragments of one
function.

**For prose it is pathological, and the pathology generalises:**

> If surviving regions inherit their parent document's score, then 200 returned results carry only
> *n_documents* distinct scores. Any stable sort produces contiguous per-document blocks. A top-k
> prefix therefore returns whole documents rather than the best passages, and evidence spread across
> documents is unreachable **at any k**.

**[measured]** 200 results carried **19 distinct scores**; 181 of 200 were duplicates of one of 19
parents.

This is a **score-granularity failure**. It is invisible to almost every standard metric. Accuracy
looks fine. Recall@200 looks fine. **Only recall@10 exposes it**, because only a small-k prefix
reveals that the ordering is degenerate.

**The fix is passage-level retrieval done properly** (Callan, SIGIR 1994; modern form: Dense X
Retrieval, EMNLP 2024). Each passage competes on its own score, with a breadth constraint so document
coverage survives:

```
input: scored regions R, budget k
  S ← ∅
  breadth pass: for each document d, admit d's best region while |S| < k
  merit pass:   admit remaining regions by descending score while |S| < k
output: S
```

The breadth pass must bind **every** selection round, not just the first. Without it, a document
whose regions all score highly monopolises the budget. **[measured]** Document coverage stayed at
18.9 per query while distinct scores rose from 17.1 to 84.9.

## 1.5 Context packing

Every response is bounded in bytes, enforced **during** assembly rather than after. In IR terms this
is **snippet generation under a length budget**, the same problem as building a search-results
snippet, except the consumer is a model with a context window rather than a human scanning a page.

**The subtlety worth knowing.** The ceiling must be computed on the **text the consumer reads**, not
on the serialised response. Bounding on the wrong quantity lets an expansion pass shrink the payload
while growing delivered text by 90%, because the structural envelope of a result is far larger than a
prose snippet. **[measured]** This exact mistake happened and produced a result that looked rigorous
and was not.

---

# PART 2 — Information retrieval fundamentals you need

## 2.1 Sparse retrieval

**TF-IDF** weights a term by how often it appears in a document against how rare it is in the corpus.

**BM25** is the standard refinement, with two parameters: `k1` controls term-frequency saturation
(the tenth occurrence of a word matters less than the second), and `b` controls length normalisation
(how much to penalise long documents). Typical values k1 ≈ 1.2, b ≈ 0.75. **Know these; you will be
asked.**

**BM25F** extends this to fielded documents, weighting title, body and anchor text differently.

**Query likelihood** models retrieval as "how likely is this document's language model to generate
this query," with smoothing (Dirichlet, Jelinek-Mercer) to handle unseen terms.

## 2.2 Dense retrieval

**Bi-encoder**: encode query and document separately into vectors, retrieve by nearest neighbour.
Fast, because documents are encoded once offline. **DPR** is the canonical example; **Contriever**
and **E5** are unsupervised and instruction-tuned successors.

**Cross-encoder**: encode query and document *together*, output a relevance score. Far more accurate,
far more expensive, cannot be precomputed. **monoBERT**, **monoT5**, **RankT5**.

**The standard architecture is both**: a cheap first stage retrieves 100–1000 candidates, an
expensive reranker reorders the top of that list. This is retrieve-then-rerank, and it is the single
most important architectural pattern in modern IR.

**ColBERT** sits between them with **late interaction**: encode tokens separately, compare with a
MaxSim operator at query time. More accurate than a bi-encoder, cheaper than a cross-encoder, at the
cost of a much larger index.

**Learned sparse** (**SPLADE**, **uniCOIL**) predicts term weights with a transformer but stores them
in an inverted index, so it inherits sparse retrieval's infrastructure and efficiency while learning
its weights.

**Hybrid** combines sparse and dense scores, usually by **reciprocal rank fusion** (RRF), which is
robust because it fuses ranks rather than incomparable score scales.

## 2.3 Approximate nearest neighbour

Dense retrieval needs ANN search at scale. **HNSW** (hierarchical navigable small world graphs) is
the dominant in-memory method; **IVF-PQ** (inverted file with product quantisation) trades accuracy
for a much smaller footprint. FAISS, ScaNN, and every vector database implement one or both.

The tradeoff to be able to discuss: **recall against latency against memory**. HNSW is fast and
accurate and memory-hungry; PQ compresses aggressively and loses recall.

## 2.4 Chunking and granularity

This is where a great deal of practical RAG quality lives.

- **Fixed-size chunking with overlap** is the default and it is arbitrary; it splits semantic units.
- **Syntactic chunking** uses structure (headings, functions, paragraphs). What entire-graph does.
- **Parent-document retrieval**: retrieve small chunks for precision, return the larger parent for
  context. Standard industrial practice.
- **RAPTOR** (ICLR 2024) builds a hierarchical tree by recursive clustering and summarisation, then
  retrieves across levels.
- **Late chunking** embeds the long document first, then splits, so chunk embeddings carry
  document-level context.
- **Dense X Retrieval** (EMNLP 2024) established empirically that finer units beat passages, and
  that the advantage **widens under a fixed context budget**.

## 2.5 Diversification

**MMR** (Carbonell and Goldstein 1998) is the canonical algorithm: iteratively select the document
maximising λ·relevance − (1−λ)·max_similarity_to_already_selected.

Production systems implement cruder versions: **site collapsing**, per-domain caps, deduplication by
near-identical content. entire-graph's one-per-file rule is the degenerate extreme, which is exactly
what made it fail on prose.

---

# PART 3 — Evaluation and metrics

## 3.1 The metrics

**Precision@k** — of the top k, what fraction are relevant.
**Recall@k** — of all relevant items, what fraction appear in the top k.
**MRR** — mean reciprocal rank of the *first* relevant result. Good when one right answer exists.
**MAP** — mean average precision, averages precision at every relevant position.
**nDCG** — discounted cumulative gain, normalised. **The standard when relevance is graded** rather
than binary, and the one to name by default.

**Evidence density** (gold items per 1,000 characters returned) is not standard but is the metric
that stops "return everything" from looking like good retrieval. **[measured]** One system returned a
single unit containing **109% of the source conversation**, scoring near the top on recall while
ranking last on density. Without a density measure it looks like a strong retriever.

## 3.2 The decomposition that matters most

In a RAG pipeline, an end-to-end accuracy number conflates **retrieval** with **generation**. Always
separate them:

```
P(correct | gold evidence retrieved)   ← generation quality
P(gold evidence retrieved)             ← retrieval quality
```

**[measured]** Across all seven systems tested, **P(correct | gold retrieved) was 0.96 to 0.97**.
The reader was saturated. Every accuracy difference between systems was a retrieval difference
wearing a disguise.

**This is the single most useful diagnostic in the pack.** If generation is saturated, stop tuning
prompts and work on retrieval. If retrieval recall is high and accuracy is low, the reverse.

## 3.3 Budget-matched comparison

**A retrieval budget expressed as top-k equalises item count, not context volume.** Two systems at
`top_k = 200` can deliver wildly different amounts of text if their units differ in size.

**[measured]** At the same nominal budget, systems delivered from 7,418 to 82,419 characters per
question. At tight cutoffs the disparity reached **7.9×**. Any "same budget" claim that does not
report characters is not a fair comparison, and any win at small k under item-matching may be a
prompt-size artifact.

**Report accuracy against delivered characters, not against k.**

---

# PART 4 — Measurement discipline

This section is what separates a credible evaluation from a plausible one. Most of it was learned by
getting it wrong first.

## 4.1 Establish a noise floor before believing any margin

Run one system twice under identical settings.

**[measured]** Two identical configurations of the same system scored **93.83 and 93.57**, a 0.65
point spread, and **disagreed on 11.3% of individual answers**. Any margin below that is not a
result.

## 4.2 Paired deltas decay with sample size

**[measured]** A paired margin of **+2.00 points at n=400 became −0.39 at n=1,540**, reproduced
independently on three separate arms. Question difficulty correlates with run order, so both arms
fall as n grows, but not equally.

**Consequence: never report an effect from a subset.** Interim readings are for health checks, not
effect sizes.

## 4.3 Measurement drift across time

**[measured]** An identical configuration re-run 26 hours apart differed by **2.21 points**, with
byte-identical retrieval on 299 of 300 questions. The systems had not changed; the shared endpoint's
behaviour had.

**Consequence: run the arms you intend to compare concurrently.** Cross-time comparison is unsafe.

## 4.4 Pre-register the decision rule

Write down, before the numbers land, what you will publish at each outcome. Otherwise you will pick
the analysis that flatters you without noticing you did.

We registered: p < 0.05 publishes as significant; 0.05 ≤ p < 0.10 publishes as a non-significant
lead; p ≥ 0.10 publishes as a tie. And explicitly forbade switching metric, switching cutoff,
post-hoc exclusions, or replicating until significant.

## 4.5 The statistics

**McNemar's test** is the right test for paired binary outcomes: two systems on the same items, each
either right or wrong. It uses only the **discordant pairs** (cases where they disagree). Do not use
an unpaired t-test on paired data.

**Bootstrap confidence intervals** where the sampling distribution is unclear.

**Power and minimum detectable effect.** If you are claiming a null, you must say what effect you
could have detected. **[measured]** Resolving a four-question difference on a 96-question category
would need roughly **470 questions**.

## 4.6 Infrastructure defects that look like results

Every one of these produced a plausible false number in our campaign:

| defect | mechanism | cost |
|---|---|---|
| concurrency default | 100 workers at 200 rpm saturated the endpoint; nearly every call timed out and retried | throughput collapsed to near zero |
| state under `/tmp` | systemd wipes it on boot | multi-GB state lost |
| resume into empty buffer | checkpoints on disk, retrieval buffer in memory; resumed run searched nothing and answered confidently | **13.77 points** |
| connect vs read timeout | the configured timeout applied only to reads; a hardcoded 15s connect timeout failed every worker's first call | **0.65 points**, larger than the effect under study |
| cross-window comparison | endpoint behaviour drifts | **2.21 points** |

**The lesson to carry: audit the harness before blaming the system.** In this campaign every
withdrawn headline died of a measurement bug, not a bad idea.

## 4.7 Fix your competitors' bugs

**[measured]** Three of six competing systems were suppressed by defects in their own shipped code:

- an argument passed as `limit` to a signature expecting `top_k`, absorbed silently into `**kwargs`,
  capping retrieval at 20 instead of 200 — worth **+6.04 points** once fixed
- state persisted to disk while the retrieval buffer stayed in memory — **+13.77 points**
- a BM25 path that excluded its own node type from results, returning nothing on prose —
  **structurally zero → 91.30**

A competitor scoring near zero is a broken integration until proven otherwise. Fixing their bugs in
their favour is both correct and the strongest credibility signal an evaluation can carry.

---

# PART 5 — The agent-memory landscape

## 5.1 The systems

| system | approach | venue |
|---|---|---|
| Mem0 | LLM fact extraction and consolidation | ECAI 2025 |
| Zep / Graphiti | temporal knowledge graph | arXiv |
| Cognee | multi-stage cognify pipeline per chunk | no paper found |
| MemGPT / Letta | agent-controlled archival passages | arXiv |
| A-MEM | associative memory over extracted notes | NeurIPS 2025 |
| HippoRAG 2 | associative retrieval, neurobiologically motivated | ICML 2025 |
| LightMem | efficient memory, large online token reduction | ICLR 2026 |

**All of them call a model at ingest**, most per stored item.

## 5.2 The counter-current, which is the important part

A recent line argues the inference is not load-bearing:

- **DMF** — deterministic memory, comparable accuracy, large token reduction
- **Zero-Mem** — no model call outside final answering
- **ReFind** (August 2026) — a purely **lexical** index over the *unmodified* archive, building no
  semantic structure, tops MemoryAgentBench and reaches 93.2 on LongMemEval-S
- **Better Call Grep** (ISSTA 2026) — on code, naive lexical retrieval "achieves performance
  comparable to sophisticated graph-based baselines"

**Both of the last two attack structured retrieval on index-construction overhead.** That is the
argument to be ready for, and the honest response is not to dispute the accuracy half but to observe
that the attack targets a cost a zero-inference index does not incur.

## 5.3 The benchmarks

**LoCoMo** — ten multi-session conversations, 1,540 questions, four categories. **Known to have a
defective answer key**: an independent audit found 99 score-corrupting errors (6.4%), implying a
ceiling near 93.6% for a perfect system.

**LongMemEval** (ICLR 2025) — 500 questions, five ability categories. Notable for **reporting
human-judge agreement**, which almost nothing else in this literature does.

**MemoryAgentBench**, **BEAM** — newer, less established.

---

# PART 6 — What we measured

Full LoCoMo, 1,540 questions, shared reader and judge, `top_k = 200`, zero dropped questions.

| system | accuracy | index calls | index tokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| entire-graph | **94.74** | **0** | **0** |
| mem0 OSS | 93.83 | 5,882 | 50.85M |
| cognee | 92.86 | 11,749 | 12.35M |
| cmm | 91.30 | 0 | 0 |
| graphify | 87.34 | 0 | 0 |
| letta | 80.58 | not projectable | not projectable |
| supermemory | 77.60 | not measurable | not measurable |

Margin over mem0: **+0.91 points, McNemar p = 0.125** against a 0.65 point noise floor. Reported as a
ranking, **not** as a significant difference.

**Recall@10: .820 against .568** for the next measurable system. The largest separation measured.

**Index construction: seconds versus hours.** Deterministic systems build in 4 to 7 seconds;
extraction systems in 3,373 to 20,478 seconds. Three orders of magnitude.

**Cost measurement method**: a transparent HTTP proxy forwarding requests unchanged and recording
only token accounting, validated against a competitor's own internal meter with exact agreement.
Linearity tested with two conversations of different length per system rather than assumed.

---

# PART 7 — Interview material

## 7.1 The diagnosis story

*"Our retriever returned 200 results but they carried only 19 distinct relevance scores. I traced it
to candidate selection admitting one region per file, which is correct for code and wrong for prose.
Because promoted regions inherited their parent's score, a stable sort collapsed the ranking into
contiguous per-document blocks, so any top-k prefix returned whole documents rather than the best
passages. Cross-document evidence was structurally unreachable at any k. I made the section the
retrieval unit with a two-pass rule that preserves document coverage. Multi-hop accuracy went from
88.30 to 93.97, and the response got 11.4% smaller because the old build was computing regions and
discarding them unread. I verified code search was unaffected with 30 identical full-payload
comparisons."*

**Why it works:** it is a mechanism, not a metric. It shows you can reason about ordering semantics,
and it ends with a verification step.

## 7.2 The instrumentation story

*"The published cost comparisons in this space are wall-clock, which measures the wrong thing when
ingest is interleaved with querying. I built a transparent proxy in front of the inference endpoint
that forwards requests unchanged and records only token accounting, so the measurement is identical
across systems by construction. I validated it against one competitor's own internal meter and got
exact agreement. Then I found my own instrument had a failure curve under concurrency, from 0% at two
arms to 56% at six, because it opened a fresh connection per request. I rebuilt it on a connection
pool and re-measured. The final numbers are zero tokens against 50.85 million."*

**Why it works:** you distrusted your own tooling and proved it wrong before it produced a headline.

## 7.3 The judgement story

*"Our system scored 94.74 against the strongest competitor's 93.83 on identical questions in the same
window. I reported it as a tie. The margin was 0.91 points, McNemar p = 0.125, and I had established
by running one system against itself that the noise floor was 0.65 points. I also found that paired
deltas on that harness decay with sample size, from +2.00 at n=400 to −0.39 at n=1,540. We withdrew
five of our own claims during the campaign and fixed three competitors' bugs in their favour."*

**Why it works:** almost nobody volunteers this, and it is the strongest possible signal that the
numbers you *do* report can be trusted.

---

# PART 8 — Your gaps and how to close them

**What this work does not cover:**

1. **Learned retrieval.** No embeddings trained, no reranker, no fine-tuning. This is the biggest gap
   for an IR role, since much of the field is exactly this.
2. **Serving engineering.** No sharding, no latency SLOs under load, no index refresh at scale, no
   ANN tuning.
3. **Online evaluation.** Offline benchmarks only; no A/B on live traffic, no interleaving, no
   click models.

**The single project that closes gap 1**, and it slots into the harness you already have:

You will shortly have a **BM25 lexical floor** and a **structural first stage** measured on identical
questions. Add a **cross-encoder reranker** over the candidates from each. That gives you sparse,
structural, and learned reranking on one evaluation, and it directly answers the question the two
hostile papers raise. Measure nDCG and latency alongside accuracy, and report the accuracy-per-
millisecond tradeoff.

That is a two-week project and it is the difference between "evaluated retrieval systems" and "built
and evaluated retrieval systems."

---

# Glossary

**ANN** — approximate nearest neighbour search. HNSW, IVF-PQ.
**Bi-encoder** — query and document encoded separately; fast, precomputable.
**BM25** — the standard sparse ranking function. Parameters k1 (saturation), b (length norm).
**Cross-encoder** — query and document encoded together; accurate, expensive, not precomputable.
**Discordant pairs** — items where two systems disagree; the only ones McNemar's test uses.
**Evidence density** — relevant items recovered per unit of text returned.
**Late interaction** — token-level comparison at query time (ColBERT).
**MMR** — maximal marginal relevance; the canonical diversification algorithm.
**MRR** — mean reciprocal rank of the first relevant result.
**nDCG** — normalised discounted cumulative gain; the standard graded-relevance metric.
**Parent-document retrieval** — retrieve small units for precision, return larger parents for context.
**RRF** — reciprocal rank fusion; combines rankings robustly across incomparable score scales.
**Score-granularity failure** — too few distinct scores, so a stable sort produces degenerate
ordering. Visible only at small k.
**Sparse retrieval** — inverted-index term matching. BM25 and relatives.

A trained reranker over those candidates, measured with nDCG and latency, is a two-week project on infrastructure that already exists.

**Where I'd push back on the framing:** don't try to look complete. The strongest thing you have is not breadth, it's that you can say "I reported a tie when the number said we won, and here is why." Lead with that and treat the reranker as the thing you're building next.

**Yes, and one of the three is worth doing on product merit, not just to close a CV gap.**

**Cross-encoder reranking — genuinely valuable.** Brain currently reranks with the same embeddings it retrieves with, which means the reranker cannot see anything the retriever missed. It re-sorts using the same signal. A cross-encoder encodes query and passage jointly and typically buys **5 to 15 nDCG points** over a bi-encoder first stage in the published literature. That is a real quality improvement, and it fits brain's architecture cleanly because RRF already produces a candidate list waiting to be reordered.

**The catch you'd have to face honestly:** it breaks the zero-inference property. Brain already calls an embedder, so it is not strictly zero-inference at query time, but a cross-encoder is a forward pass **per candidate**, so reranking 100 candidates is 100 forward passes. On a local endpoint that is meaningful latency. The honest framing is a quality-latency knob: rerank the top 20, not the top 200.

**ANN — do not add it.** Brute-force cosine is correct at brain's scale and the source already says so. Adding HNSW below a hundred thousand vectors buys you index build time, memory, a tuning surface, and recall loss, in exchange for solving a problem you do not have. **Adding it would make brain worse.** It only becomes right if brain's corpus grows by two orders of magnitude, and at that point it is a real project rather than a checkbox.

**Online evaluation — the highest product value of the three, and the least CV-shaped.** Brain is used by agents. Whether a retrieved fact was actually *used* in the resulting work is observable, and nobody in this space measures it. That would be a genuine differentiator and it is closer to instrumentation, which is the thing you have already proven you can do.

**Where I'd push back on "graph is over."**

Graph is not over. Its evaluation is over. There are two open threads worth more than any of the above: the **PR still needs merging**, and the **powered replication** at n≈650 that would turn its weakest section into its strongest is still unrun. And there is a live open question in the paper itself, the amortisation frontier, which is the read-write ratio at which paying a model at index time earns back its cost. Nobody has formalised that, we have both axes measured, and it is the one genuinely unclaimed theoretical slot the literature search found.

**If you want one thing that improves the product and closes the gap simultaneously:** the cross-encoder over brain's RRF output, measured on the same harness against the BM25 arm and the structural arm. Same evaluation, three architectures, nDCG and latency reported together.

## The robustness check — the ranking holds under a different reader

```
reader gpt-5.6-sol   eg 94.48  mem0 94.03   +0.45   disc 40/33

That answers the objection I flagged as most likely to sink a submission. It is not a significance result and I won't present it as one, but "the ranking is not an artifact of one reader" is now measured rather than assumed. **Lucene** is the open-source search library that Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Solr are all built on. It's the industrial reference implementation of BM25 and inverted-index search — when someone says "we use BM25 in production," they almost always mean Lucene's.

**We already used its analysis pipeline.** The agent's tokeniser is Lucene's chain exactly: lowercase, alphanumeric split, English stopwords, Snowball stemming. What differs is the scorer — `rank_bm25`'s `BM25Okapi` rather than Lucene's `BM25Similarity`, with the same k1=1.2 and b=0.75.

**Swapping in real Lucene would change almost nothing.** The two differ only in the IDF formula's edge handling and Lucene's quantised length normalisation. You'd spend a day on PyLucene or an Elasticsearch container to move the number by a fraction of a point. **The granularity experiment is worth ten times more**, because that one can actually overturn our claim.

content.text:
No LME competitor arms exist locally, and the paper carries 21 refs and a placeholder author block. Here's the honest gap.

## 5 blockers

**1. One benchmark.** LoCoMo only. This is the single most common desk-reject for a systems+eval paper at TKDE — reviewers will not accept a retrieval claim resting on 1,540 questions from ten conversations. LME exists for eg alone at 89.80 with **no matched competitor arms**, so it isn't usable yet. Needs mem0, cognee, BM25 re-run on the same spine. ~2–3 h/arm question phase, plus mem0's ~5.7 h ingest. **~2 days wall clock.**

**2. The headline is not significant.** 94.74 vs 93.83 is +0.91 at p=0.125, CI [−0.19, +2.01] — it crosses zero, and the running second-reader agent has already re-confirmed that against the banked labels. A reviewer will find this in ten minutes. Two ways out, and they compose: make the **primary claim the cost axis** (0 vs 50.85M ingest tokens is an absolute, not a statistical estimate) with accuracy as parity-or-better; and buy power from blocker 1. The BM25 margin (+2.86, p=5.7e-07) already survives on its own.

**3. BM25 at matched granularity.** This is the experiment that can overturn the paper. Our mechanism claim is that *granularity* drives the result. BM25 currently indexes at a different unit — if BM25 at turn+session granularity closes the 2.86pp, the mechanism section is wrong. Reviewers will ask for exactly this. It has to run before submission, not in rebuttal. **~4 h.**

**4. Related work is conference-length.** 21 refs. TKDE surveys expect 40–60 with an actual taxonomy — extraction-based vs structural vs lexical memory, and where we sit. **~1 day writing.**

**5. Metadata and artifact.** Author names, affiliation, emails, ORCID — I can't invent these. Plus PR #104 merged, a Zenodo DOI for the artifact, and a licence choice. **Needs you.**

## Bottom line

**~3–4 days**, and only two of the five are real gates: the second benchmark and the granularity control. Blocker 3 is the one I'd run first, because a bad result there changes what the paper says rather than just delaying it.

The system half — Sections II–VI, the three architecture figures, the reproduction protocol — is submission-grade now. The evaluation half is one benchmark and one control short.

content.text:
**$42 to $786 for the one ingest**, depending on rate card. Mid-frontier pricing puts it around **$130**.

The reason the range is that wide is the split, which I hadn't broken out before:

| | input | output | out % |
|---|---|---|---|
| mem0 | 50.33M | 0.52M | **1.0%** |
| cognee | 8.84M | 3.51M | 28.4% |

mem0's 50.85M is **99% input** — it re-sends a large prompt per chunk (8,556 in, 89 out) and gets back a terse extraction. Input is the cheap side, so the headline token count overstates the dollar gap.

That produces an inversion worth knowing: cognee uses **4.1× fewer tokens** than mem0, but because 28% of them are output, it's only **2.3× cheaper** at premium rates. Token counts don't rank the same way dollars do — and the paper currently quotes only tokens.

The figure that generalizes is per-chunk, since the corpus here is tiny (5,882 chunks = ten conversations):

| corpus | mem0 @ mid frontier | entire-graph |
|---|---|---|
| this benchmark (5.9k chunks) | $131 | $0 |
| 100k chunks | $2,228 | $0 |
| 1M chunks | $22,280 | $0 |

I'm pricing at bands rather than naming a figure because I don't have a public rate card for the `gpt-5.6-terra` deployment we metered — the token counts are measured, the dollars are a conversion I can't source. If you want a single number in the paper, tell me the rate and I'll put it in §6a.

The argument that survives regardless of rate card is the recurrence: that cost lands again on **every corpus change**, and entire-graph's side of the column is zero at every scale and every price.

Abstract—We present entire-graph, a structural index that makes a corpus queryable by 66 grammar-based parsing alone. It performs no language model calls and no network requests at 67 index time, and produces a byte-identical index for a given corpus state. The system parses source 68 files and prose documents into a graph of symbols, types, routes and document sections together with 69 the relations between them, and answers queries by hybrid lexical and structural ranking under an 70 enforced context budget. We describe the index model, the identity scheme that keeps symbol 71 identifiers stable across unrelated edits, the ranking and candidate-selection algorithms, and the 72 budget enforcement that bounds every response. We then report a defect in candidate selection that 73 we found, characterised and corrected: admitting one candidate per file is correct for source code 74 and wrong for prose, and it caused 200 returned results to carry only 19 distinct relevance scores, 75 making cross-document evidence assembly structurally impossible. Finally we evaluate the system on a 76 conversational-memory benchmark against six purpose-built memory systems, where it places first 77 while consuming zero tokens to build its index against a measured 50.85 million for the 78 strongest competitor. Against a standard lexical baseline built at the same zero cost, it leads by 79 2.86 points at p = 5.7 × 10−7. Because index construction is free on 80 both sides, that comparison isolates retrieval quality from cost.
