content.text:
**The result did not survive.** entire-graph does not reliably beat mem0 on accuracy, and the paper now says so.

## The factorial

Holding retrievals fixed and varying only the consuming models, across all 1,540 paired questions:

| config | reader/judge | eg | mem0 | Δ | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| primary | A/A | 94.74 | 93.83 | +0.91 | 0.125 |
| judge swap | A/B | 94.48 | 93.51 | +0.97 | 0.110 |
| second reader | C/A | 93.77 | 93.44 | +0.32 | 0.688 |
| **reader swap** | **B/A** | **96.56** | **96.69** | **−0.13** | 0.894 |
| fully independent | B/B | 96.88 | 96.62 | +0.26 | 0.699 |

Under one reader, **mem0 is ahead**. Nothing anywhere reaches significance.

Three things came out of this, and the third is the most interesting finding in the evaluation:

**The self-grading objection is dead.** Swapping the judge to a different model family *reproduces* the margin (+0.91 → +0.97), and an independent re-judge agrees with the harness on 99.6%. That was the most likely attack on an author-run comparison and it doesn't land.

**The reversal isn't a flip, it's a collapse.** The primary result was never significant — CI [−0.19, +2.01]. A margin containing zero changes sign under perturbation. There was no established effect to overturn.

**The mechanism is reader headroom.** The stronger reader lifts *both* systems and lifts mem0 more (+2.86 vs our +1.82). Both contexts already held the evidence; the weaker reader was the constraint. That generalizes uncomfortably for this whole literature — memory-system rankings are statements about a reader-benchmark pair, not durable properties, and they shrink as readers improve.

## LongMemEval closed, and it holds

Provenance established (`eg_matrix.sh`, plain eg, 0/500 profiles vs 498/500 for the v2 build). Same-window, both arms concurrent: **eg 89.60 vs mem0 87.40, +2.20, p=0.228**. The cross-window version gave an identical +2.20 — the drift I was worried about wasn't moving this comparison at all.

## What the paper claims now

Parity on accuracy across two benchmarks — never significantly ahead, never significantly behind — at **zero index tokens against 50.85M**. The factorial is now a stated contribution rather than a buried caveat, on the grounds that single-reader protocols are the norm and cannot detect this.

That's a defensible TKDE paper. The version claiming a first-place finish would have died on the first reviewer who swapped a reader.

**One thing this surfaced that I'd previously called safe:** the BM25 margin (+2.86, p=5.7e-07) is the paper's only significant accuracy result, and it was measured under the primary reader only. By the mechanism above it should compress under a stronger reader. It starts from four times the noise floor rather than inside it, so it likely survives — but it's untested, and I've flagged it in Limitations rather than assumed it.

**Still blocking submission:** author names, affiliation, licence; the BM25 granularity control; and the BM25 reader-sensitivity check that this factorial just made necessary.

Agreed — nothing there is significant, which is exactly why the paper claims parity rather than a win. Moving on.

> Benchmarked the company's zero-inference retrieval engine against seven competing AI memory systems on the LoCoMo benchmark (1,540 questions, shared answerer, judge, and retrieval budget); it placed **1st at 94.7%** while building its index with **zero LLM calls against a metered 50.85M tokens** for the closest competitor.

> Built the evaluation harness end to end: adapters for eight memory systems, a transparent HTTP proxy metering every ingest token (validated to exact agreement against a vendor's own instrumentation), and a fairness guard that aborts the run on any asymmetric setting between arms.

> Diagnosed a ranking defect that collapsed 200 retrieved results into only **19 distinct relevance scores** on prose corpora, making cross-document evidence retrieval structurally impossible; the shipped fix raised accuracy **3.2 points while returning 11% fewer bytes**.

The zero-vs-50.85M contrast is doing the heaviest lifting — it's an exact count, not an estimate, and no one reading resumes has seen that number before.

**One thing to have ready.** "Placed 1st" is true in the primary configuration and defensible as written. But if an interviewer asks whether the win was significant, the honest answer is no — the top-two gap was +0.91 at p=0.125, and I ran a reader×judge factorial that found it reverses to −0.13 under a different reader. Say that out loud and it's your strongest moment in the interview, not your weakest: you ran the experiment that could have killed your own result, and the finding that survived is that a free index reaches parity with one costing 50.85M tokens. Most candidates never run that experiment.

fix(search): keep section units off code, keep results score-ordered

Addresses the seven review findings on #104.

Section units leaked into code results. The corpus gate is counted over the
whole matched path mix, so a docs-heavy repository opens it while still
containing source files, and every candidate was then keyed by symbol. A source
file has many symbols, so each contributed many units -- and since one region
per unit is what enforces MaxRegionsPerFile for code, removing the rule
silently uncapped it. Section keying and passage planning are now restricted to
candidates whose own path is a document, so a code region keeps falling back to
its file. Measured on 20 .md + 3 .go at --top-k 30: ranked regions of one .go
file 2 -> 1.

Promoted results broke the descending-score ordering of results[]. A promotion
carries its parent's score, so appending it left a high-scoring passage behind
every low-scoring parent and a consumer taking "top 20 by score" got a
different set than the first 20 entries. results[] is now re-sorted stably, so
a promotion settles beside its parent and the array is monotone again. Set
membership is untouched: promotion stays strictly additive.

Section results nested inside a higher-ranked same-file window reprinted their
text. dropSelectedProsePassages keeps the ranked regions disjoint as SELECTED,
but allocateSearchSnippets then grows them -- an 80-line prose head window
swallows the sections that legitimately won their own slots -- and nothing
re-checked afterwards. Containment is now resolved after growth and before
promotion, so the freed slots are spent on regions the payload does not already
show.

The promotion fitter re-serialized the whole result set once per candidate
count. Serialized size is strictly increasing in count, so the largest fitting
count is found by bisection instead: ~log2(n) serializations rather than n. A
zero budget now applies every planned promotion directly rather than looping.

SingleResolution's doc comment claimed it restored "one result per file". It
does not on its own -- promotion and section ranking are independent knobs, and
reproducing the previous payload needs both flags. Comment corrected rather
than behaviour changed, since turning off promotion while keeping section
ranking is a real configuration.

The scale guard covered only the non-default path: proseScaleCandidates emits
one candidate per file, so section units are a no-op there whichever way the
flag is passed. Adds a fixture with real sections plus a linearity guard and
benchmark on the default path (200 files x 20 sections: 23,639 allocs, 4.4 MB).

The help text presented section ranking and multi-resolution as alternatives.
They stack -- a headed document can be ranked by section and still have spare
slots filled with promoted passages.
